figure_candidates.label: Figure 1
figure_candidates.caption:
Figure 1. Selective apiosylation reactions catalyzed by two types of flavonoid apiosyltranserases. (A) Type I apiosyltransferase: GuApiGT catalyzes
the O-apiosylation of flavonoid 7- or 4′-O-glycosides. (B) Type II apiosyltransferase: CaApiGT catalyzes the O-apiosylation of flavonoid 3-O-
glycosides. (C) The key α-helix determines the sugar acceptor selectivity of the two types of apiosyltransferases. The pink ring and purple pentagon
represent glycosyl and apiosyl moieties, respectively.

figure_candidates.label: Figure 2
figure_candidates.caption:
Figure 2. Functional characterization of CaApiGT. (A) Picture of the C. arietinum plant, and the catalytic function of CaApiGT using astragalin (1)
as sugar acceptor. (B) High-performance liquid chromatography (HPLC) chromatograms of the enzyme catalytic reactions. Acceptor 1 was
incubated with CaApiGT and an UDP-Api supply system (UDP-GlcA, UAXS, NAD+) in pH 8.0 (50 mM NaH2PO4−Na2HPO4 buffer) at 37 °C
for 4 h. (C) (−)-ESI-MS and MS/MS spectra of astragalin 2″-O-apioside (1a). (D) Gene expression levels of CaApiGT and the contents of 1a in
the leaves of EV and CaApiGT-VIGS groups. The gene expression levels and contents are presented as the mean ± standard deviation (SD) of five
biologically independent samples (n = 5). *p < 0.05, **p < 0.01, compared with the EV group by Student’s test. (E) Picture of a positive transgenic
hairy root of C. arietinum, and LC/MS extracted ion chromatograms (EIC m/z 579.1353) of the EV and CaApiGT-overexpression groups. The
hairy roots were screened under fluorescence (LUYOR-3430, USA). DsRed, 510−540 nm. (F) De novo biosynthesis of 1a in tobacco, showing the
gene combinations and the contents of products in tobacco leaves (mg/g, dry weight). Tobacco may contain the endogenous flavonoid 3-O-
glycosyltransferases. The contents are presented as mean ± SD of three biologically independent samples (n = 3).

figure_candidates.label: Figure 3
figure_candidates.caption:
Figure 3. Substrate promiscuity of CaApiGT and PcApiGT. (A) Conversion rates of different types of flavonoid O-glycosides as substrates
catalyzed by CaApiGT and PcApiGT, respectively. The conversion rates are presented as the mean ± SD of three independent samples (n = 3).
(B) Chemical structures of substrates 1−24. Δ, products purified, and identified by NMR analysis. ∇, products identified by comparing with
reference standards.

figure_candidates.label: Figure 4
figure_candidates.caption:
Figure 4. Complex crystal structures of CaApiGT and the key amino acid residues. (A) Crystal structure of CaApiGT/UDP (PDB 9KSM). (B, C)
Composite omit electron-density maps of ligands in the crystal structures of CaApiGT/UDP/1 (PDB 9KSO), CaApiGT/UDP/2 (PDB 9KSR),
CaApiGT/UDP/7 (PDB 9KSS), CaApiGT/UMP/5 (PDB 9KSW), CaApiGT/UDP/10 (PDB 9KSX), and CaApiGT/UDP/11 (PDB 9KSY) and
their overlay images. The maps are contoured at the 1.5σ level. (D) Summary of residues that interact with different sites of sugar acceptor 1.
Hydrogen bonds are shown as black dashes. Hydrophobic interactions are shown as point-like clouds. π-Stacking interactions are shown as gray
dashes. (E) Per-residue contribution of binding energies and key residues of CaApiGT (|contribution|1.0 kcal/mol) with acceptor 1. The figure was
plotted based on the contribution values of each amino acid residue calculated by molecular mechanics generalized Born surface area (MM/GBSA)
free energy analysis. (F) Conversion rates of CaApiGT mutants were calculated using 1 as the sugar acceptor.

figure_candidates.label: Figure 5
figure_candidates.caption:
Figure 5. Mechanisms for catalytic preference toward different quercetin 3-O-glycosides by CaApiGT. (A) Conversion rates of CaApiGTWT and
CaApiGTF192Y were obtained using 2, 7, 5, 10, and 11 as sugar acceptors, respectively. The conversion rates are presented as mean ± SD of three
independent samples (n = 3). (B) Population of key criteria (points in the dashed-line frame) for the apiosylation reactivity, based on metadynamic
simulations of CaApiGT with different sugar acceptors. Acceptor 2, 16,969/20,000; acceptor 7, 15,007/20,000; acceptor 5, 10,838/2,0000;
acceptor 10, 9874/20,000; acceptor 11, 8211/20,000. (C) Binding free energy of UDP/UMP and different sugar acceptors in CaApiGT, calculated
by the Alchemical method (see method). (D) The interactions between the 192-site and 4″-OH of 11 in CaApiGTWT and CaApiGTF192Y.

figure_candidates.label: Figure 6
figure_candidates.caption:
Figure 6. Complex crystal structures of PcApiGT and the key amino acid residues. (A) Crystal structure of PcApiGT/UDP (PDB 9KSZ). (B)
Binding modes of PcApiGT with 17 and 20 (PDB 9KSV, 9KT0), respectively. (C) Summary of residues that interact with different sites of sugar
acceptor 17. Hydrogen bonds are shown as black dashes. Hydrophobic interactions are shown as point-like clouds. (D) Per-residue contribution of
binding energies and key residues of PcApiGT (|contribution|0.5 kcal/mol) with 17. The figure was plotted based on the contribution values of
each amino acid residue calculated by MM/GBSA free energy analysis. (E) Conversion rates of PcApiGT mutants were determined using 17 as the
sugar acceptor.

figure_candidates.label: Figure 7
figure_candidates.caption:
Figure 7. Mechanisms for the different sugar acceptor selectivity of CaApiGT and PcApiGT. (A) MD simulations of CaApiGT/UDP-Api/1,
CaApiGT/UDP-Api/17, PcApiGT/UDP/17, and PcApiGT/UDP-Api/1 about variations in the O−C1 distance over 300 ns. (B) Binding modes
of 1 and 17 in the pocket of CaApiGT (PDB 9KSO) and PcApiGT (PDB 9KSV), respectively. (C) Key α-helix is found in CaApiGT, PcApiGT,
and GuApiGT. 12.0 Å represents the distance from 7-OH to Glc 3″-OH of acceptor 1. 9.8 Å represents the distance from 5-OH to 4′-OH of
acceptor 1. 15.8 Å represents the distance from 4′-OH to Glc 4″-OH of acceptor 17. 4.1 Å represents the distance from 1−O to 4O of acceptor
17. (D) Key α-helices of CaApiGT (purple), PcApiGT (green), and GuApiGT (orange). (E) Comparison of the selected distance (the distance
from the centroid of the His main chain atoms, including CA, C, N, and O, to the centroid of the α-helix main chain atoms) for the three
apiosyltransferases, based on 500 ns MD simulation trajectories. (F) Relative catalytic activities of CaApiGT wild type (WT) and mutants. Y-axis
with purple background represents the relative activity using 1 as acceptor. Y-axis with green background represents the relative activity using 17 as
acceptor. These two axes have no quantitative relationships. The relative activities are presented as the mean ± SD of three independent samples (n
= 3).

figure_candidates.label: Figure 8
figure_candidates.caption:
Figure 8. Discovery of apiosyltransferases from Leguminosae plants that accept flavonoid 3-O-glycosides. (A) Sequence alignment of the key α-
helix for the eight known plant phenolic ApiGTs. Polar amino acids are shown in purple. Amino acids that could break the helix are shown in pink.
The other amino acids are colored gray. (B) Sequence alignment of the α-helix of 120 candidate leguminous apiosyltransferases, showing the
difference of two types (19 and 101 enzymes, respectively). (C) Functional characterization of AmApiGT (Astragalus membranaceus), CcApiGT
(Cajanus cajan), VrApiGT (Vigna radiata), and ApApiGT (Astragalus propinquus) using 1 as sugar acceptor. HPLC chromatograms are shown. (D)
Distribution of two types of leguminous apiosyltransferases with different substrate selectivity.
